approach_variants.name: Snow Lake Trail to Great Scott Bowl and Pineapple Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Upper Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road (about 3,100 ft), I-90 exit 52. Take the Snow Lake Trail (#1013) north; a cat track runs up the valley from the end of the lot, just left of the stream, before the tread narrows to normal trail. At roughly 1.5-1.6 miles a small signed junction splits Source Lake from Snow Lake — bear left toward Source Lake.

Cross the Source Lake basin contouring near 4,000 ft, then at about 4,400 ft you crest a lip and drop into Great Scott Bowl (also called Pineapple Basin). Work up the bowl on talus, or on snow if any remains, toward Pineapple Pass at the head of it, passing beneath the Fang — the pinnacle on the bowl's west side that carries the Edge of Time route.

The common error is here, not lower down: a boot path running around the back of the Fang leads into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth. Parties who take it have to backtrack several hundred feet through trees and rock fields to get back onto the right ground. The second error is going straight up to Pineapple Pass itself — that col is the rappel line down, not the way up.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Great Scott Bowl, scramble to the notch just SOUTH of Pineapple Pass, then contour clockwise around the Tooth's south side. The last part of that contour is short class 3-4 and is not exposed; if it feels serious you are on the wrong ground.

You are at the start when you are standing under a broad, blocky face roughly 400 ft high with an obvious big vertical crack system splitting it. The first moves are easy ramps that angle LEFT to a large rectangular block, then back right into that crack system. About 100 ft up, the first belay is a slung rock horn with a balanced, flat-topped block sitting on it — that block is the confirmation you are on the standard line.

Two negative markers. If you are looking up a steep, narrow gully rather than an open face, you are in the gully between the Fang and the Tooth, one formation short — go back down and continue around. And if you scrambled straight up into a notch with rappel slings hanging above you, you are standing at Pineapple Pass on the descent route; downclimb and take the next notch south, then contour.

In early season a steeper gully runs up toward the base of the face. Do not use it unless it is filled with snow.
hazards: loose talus underfoot the whole length of Great Scott Bowl
steep sustained snow slope below Pineapple Pass in early season - axe, sometimes crampons
moat, and in some years a cornice, where the bowl's snow meets rock at the pass
rockfall from parties above on a face that is often busy
no reliable water past the Source Lake outlet

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring, snow-covered Alpental valley
approach_variants.notes:
Once there is meaningful snow the summer tread is not the route. The talus slopes the summer trail crosses are the Alpental valley's avalanche chutes — seventeen of them are counted along its length — and the winter line instead climbs the valley on the south side of the South Fork Snoqualmie toward Source Lake rather than following the summer switchbacks across those paths.

From below Source Lake, traverse up into Great Scott Bowl, typically on an upward-traversing line on the west side of the bowl passing beneath the Fang, and join whatever track leads to Pineapple Pass. Most parties cache skis or snowshoes in the bowl before the final slope.

The entire trip through the Source Lake and Snow Lake basins is avalanche terrain; this is a stability decision, not a route-finding one.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The finish is the same: the notch just south of Pineapple Pass, then a clockwise contour. Under snow the thing that decides where you can actually reach rock is the moat at the top of the bowl's snow. Probe it, and be ready to work around its edge on rock rather than force the direct step across.

With the base buried, the 'easy ramps left to a large rectangular block' start can be under snow. If you cannot find that block, you are probably below the true start — keep contouring around rather than climbing the first weakness above you, which is what puts parties into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth.
hazards: avalanche terrain the full length of the Alpental valley - roughly seventeen chutes cross the summer trail line
the summer boot path is not a safe winter line once snow is present
cornices at Pineapple Pass
moat between the snow and the rock at the top of the bowl
creek crossings near the Source Lake outlet at high early-season flow

approach_variants.name: Standard Tooth approach, then left past the Southwest Face
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the South Face approach as far as Great Scott Bowl: Alpental upper lot, Snow Lake Trail about 1.5-1.6 miles to the Source Lake junction, bear left, cross the Source Lake basin near 4,000 ft, crest the lip into Great Scott Bowl around 4,400 ft, and climb the bowl toward Pineapple Pass beneath the Fang.

Rather than finishing at the notch south of the pass and contouring to the South Face, this line stays lower and further left (west), working past the Southwest Face along the base of the west-facing wall.

The Fang is the formation that catches people out. A boot path around its back side leads up into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth; from there, getting to the Tooth Fairy means backtracking down and picking a way through rough climbers' paths in the trees and across the rock fields.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Tooth Fairy is a bolted line on the west-facing wall, and the bolts are the test. Traverse left along the base past the Southwest Face until you are under a wall with a line of fixed protection running up it — if the rock above you is blocky and takes only gear, you are still on the Southwest Face or have drifted round toward the South Face.

If you are standing in a narrow gully with the Fang on one side and the Tooth on the other, you are on the wrong side of the Fang: go back down rather than up.

In early season a moat between the snow of the bowl and the rock at the base can force extra scrambling to reach the first bolt; that moat is normal here, not a sign you are in the wrong place.
hazards: moat between snow and rock at the base in early season
loose talus in Great Scott Bowl
rockfall from parties on the South Face and Southwest Face above and right
the boot path behind the Fang leads to the wrong gully

approach_variants.name: Alpental valley to the northeast basin (winter)
approach_variants.season: Dec-Mar, and into spring on firm snow
approach_variants.notes:
From the Alpental upper lot (about 3,100 ft), go up the valley on the left side of the creek toward Source Lake, following the Source Lake line and whatever ski or boot track exists. In winter this means the valley bottom rather than the summer switchbacks, which cross the valley's avalanche chutes.

Beyond Source Lake, climb the snow finger into the basin on the Tooth's northeast side, then continue up the snow slope beneath the face. Skis are normally cached at the bottom of that slope.

Route-finding above the talus is cairn and boot-track only — there is no maintained tread — so fresh snow or a whiteout removes the only navigational aid you have.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at the foot of a distinct gully at the top of the snow slope on the northeast aspect. Pitch one climbs that gully; pitch two continues to the ridge crest above it; pitch three begins from a TREE anchor on the ridge.

That tree is the confirmation. If the ground above your gully leads onto a bare rock rib with no trees on it, you have gone up the wrong feature — drop back to the snow and traverse. Likewise, if you are still on open snow with nothing gully-shaped above, you are short of the base; the slope continues.

The second pitch is the one to think about before committing: parties report thin ice, long runouts, and balancy mixed slab where screws and pickets are hard to place. Deciding at the base whether it is in condition is the real judgement call.
hazards: Source Lake basin and the slopes below the Tooth have a documented avalanche accident history and are rated challenging avalanche terrain
the summer path is not a safe line once snow is present
thin, poorly protectable ice on the second pitch with long runouts
creek crossings near the Source Lake outlet at high flow
no maintained tread above the talus - navigation is by cairn and boot track only

approach_variants.name: Alpental valley to the Thumb Tack, then over the northeast ridge
approach_variants.season: Dec-Mar, below-freezing conditions after a thaw
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the upper Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road. Head up the Alpental valley, on the old ski-area cat track for the first stretch and then on trail, toward Source Lake. The maintained tread effectively ends at Source Lake around 3,700-3,740 ft.

If stability allows, climb the open slopes at the head of the valley and make a rising traverse into the cirque under Chair's east face, finishing at a freestanding rock called the Thumb Tack. That rock is the one unambiguous fix on the whole approach — use it as your reference, because everything above it is decided by aspect rather than by tread.

From the Thumb Tack, go north up a gully to gain the Northeast Ridge. Take the gully rather than attacking the ridge directly from the northeast. This gully is a known avalanche path and has killed climbers.

Once on the ridge, follow it to the buttress and round onto the north side of the mountain.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The single most important thing: the north face is NOT reached by climbing straight up the head of the Alpental cirque. You get onto it by crossing the northeast ridge first and coming round. A party grinding up the snow at the back of the cirque with the east face above them is under the wrong aspect entirely.

Once on the north side, the route starts roughly halfway across the face at a prominent open book — a corner with a gully feeding into it. Pitch one takes that corner on thin alpine ground; pitch two goes up steep snow and ice to a TREE belay. The tree is your confirmation you picked the right corner.

If you are standing under a continuous, featureless snow apron with no corner system above it, you have stopped short — keep traversing across the face. If you are past the halfway point of the face with the summit block directly overhead, you have gone too far.

The route is only worth starting in below-freezing conditions, ideally after a thaw has consolidated the ice and snow; on the wrong day the corner is unprotectable slush over rock.
hazards: the gully from the Thumb Tack to the northeast ridge is an avalanche path with a fatal accident history (two deaths in 1996)
avalanche paths cross the approach the length of the Alpental valley
route is only in condition below freezing after a thaw
moat at the base of the face late in the season
creek crossing near Source Lake at high flow

approach_variants.name: Source Lake basin to the divide (summer and fall rock)
approach_variants.notes:
Upper Alpental lot, I-90 exit 52. Snow Lake Trail up the valley — the first stretch is the old ski-area cat track — to the fork at about 1.5 miles, then left/west toward Source Lake, where the maintained trail ends near 3,700-3,740 ft.

Leave the tread and head northwest into the basin below Chair's east face on climbers' path, talus and heather. The Thumb Tack, a freestanding rock in the basin, is the landmark to aim for; parties commonly reach it in about two hours from the car.

At the Thumb Tack there is a genuine fork in what you do next. Continuing up the basin takes you to the foot of the east face. For the Northeast Buttress, angle sharply RIGHT from the Thumb Tack and scramble rocky heather slopes and ledges to the top of the divide, then walk along the NORTH side of the divide to the base of the buttress. That line is less obvious than the gully but easier and less exposed.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start is unmistakable once you have it in view, and every route description carries a photo of it: a blocky S-shaped gully, sometimes described as an open book, beginning just down and RIGHT of the divide. It climbs, curves right, then straightens again and finishes in a clump of trees. Two pitches of gully and chimney.

The clump of trees at the top of the S is the confirmation. If the gully in front of you runs straight with no rightward curve, and nothing green at its top, it is not the route.

In poor visibility, take the Thumb Tack as your last certain position and navigate from there: sharply right and up to the divide, then everything else happens on the divide's north side. If you are on the south or east side of the divide looking at the east face, you have not crossed over yet.

Above the gully the buttress continues on blocky low-angle rock, angling left across exposed slabby ledges toward another cluster of trees near the prow.
hazards: loose rock on the heather-and-ledge scramble up to the divide
the basin sits under avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain
rockfall onto the gully from parties above
no water above the Source Lake outlet

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring, on snow
approach_variants.notes:
Same line up the valley, but in snow the summer tread is abandoned and parties skin or boot the valley bottom to Source Lake, then up into the basin, commonly reaching the Thumb Tack shortly after first light. Skis are cached in the basin.

In snow the approach gully from the basin up toward the buttress is itself the hazard: it is a classic early-season slide path, and trip reports from this basin describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity and wind loading. Rope, axe and crampons usually come out from the basin onward rather than at the base of the route, because the approach gully is exposed enough on its own.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Same S-shaped gully, curving right and finishing in trees. Under snow the curve is easier to read from a distance than close up, so pick the line out from the basin before you commit to the divide, and hold that picture.

The trees at the top of the S are what stay visible when the rock is plastered. If you are at the foot of a straight snow runnel with no trees above it, you are on a different feature.

If the ground you are on is exposed and you have not yet crossed to the north side of the divide, stop — the gully line direct to the ridge is steeper and more exposed than the walk along the divide's north side, and it is not the recommended way to the base.
hazards: the approach gully to the buttress is a known early-season slide path
wind loading and wet-slab activity reported repeatedly in this basin
deep postholing on the basin approach
avalanche terrain the length of the Alpental valley below

approach_variants.name: Source Lake and the WNW gully into the east-face basin
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; an axe is useful in shoulder-season snow
approach_variants.notes:
Upper Alpental lot (about 3,100 ft) via I-90 exit 52. A cat track leaves the end of the lot and runs up the valley just left of the stream; the Snow Lake trail forks at roughly 1.5 miles — take the left/west branch toward Source Lake.

About half a mile along that branch, look for a fairly narrow rocky gully heading west-northwest starting around 4,200 ft. Depending on the season it holds snow, with water running down it. Climb the gully.

Around 4,800 ft you reach a small cliff; work through the notch there, then cross the basin beyond on climbers' path or snow, heading southwest straight at Chair's east face.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Go PAST the Thumb Tack. The Thumb Tack is a freestanding rock sitting in the middle of the basin and it is a waypoint, not the base — parties that stop and rack up there are several hundred feet low and one bench short of the wall. From the Thumb Tack, continue up the basin to the foot of the east face proper, around 5,500 ft.

The other confusion at that rock is directional: if you turned sharply right at the Thumb Tack and started scrambling heather and ledges toward a divide, you are on the Northeast Buttress approach, not the East Face. For the East Face you keep going straight up the basin with the wall filling the view ahead.

You are at the base when the basin runs out against a continuous face rising directly above you and the ground underfoot changes from basin talus to loose scree banked against rock.
hazards: snow and running water in the approach gully around 4,200 ft
loose scree on the final stretch to the wall
rockfall in the basin below the face
the descent gully off the summit drops east to a notch in the southeast ridge - do not confuse it with the approach gully

approach_variants.name: Talus cone below the west face
approach_variants.notes:
The west face rises above the houses on the Alpental access road. Every road along it carrying a 'Strasse' name is private, and the Alpental Community Club has since 2021 prohibited both driving and walking on them; climbers report being confronted. The talus cone under the face therefore has to be reached by a line that does not cross private land, and there is no established or signed path to it — this is the part of the approach with no fixed answer.

Once on the talus, make a rising traverse up toward the far left (north) end of the west face's talus field. At the top end of the field there is a rocky stream bed, which may be dry depending on the season; that streambed marks the north end of the talus and is the last realistic water.

Wear a helmet on the talus. Climber-triggered rockfall here is a real hazard, from your own party as much as from anyone above.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the top of the talus cone you scramble a couple of hundred feet of loose, mossy, dirty slab before any roped climbing. That dirty scrambling is part of the approach, not the route — the base of the climb is where it ends against the face proper.

The first pitch wanders about 100 ft of low fourth to low fifth class to a TREE belay. The tree is the confirmation. If you are 100 ft up and there is nothing to belay off, you are not on the line.

Negative marker: the rocky, usually dry streambed marks the far NORTH end of the talus field. If you are south of it and the wall above you is short and clean with bolts on it, you have drifted round to the sport climbing at the base of Guye's south wall and are on a different aspect of the mountain.

Apart from the traverse pitch higher up, the rock on this face is generally poor and loose. Loose rock low down is normal here and is not evidence you are off route.
hazards: no established approach to the talus - the direct approach crosses private roads that residents forbid, and climbers have been confronted
climber-triggered rockfall on the talus and on the mossy slabs
a couple of hundred feet of loose dirty slab scrambled unroped before the climbing starts
generally poor rock quality on the face
no reliable water past the streambed at the north end of the talus

approach_variants.name: Talus cone below the west face
approach_variants.notes:
Same problem and same ground as the rest of the west face. The roads named 'Strasse' off the Alpental access road are private; since 2021 the Alpental Community Club has forbidden both driving and walking on them, and climbers have been confronted by residents. The talus field has to be reached by a line that avoids private land, and no established path exists.

The route begins at the top of the talus cone below the face. Reckon on roughly half an hour to an hour from wherever you park to the top of the cone, and wear a helmet on the talus.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the top of the talus, a couple of hundred feet of loose, mossy, dirty slab is scrambled to reach the roped climbing; in early season a small snow cone sits at the bottom of those slabs and parties have used a nut tool as a self-belay across it. None of that is the route — the route starts where the scrambling ends.

The sequence that confirms you are on it: pitch one wanders about 100 ft of low fourth to low fifth to a tree belay; pitch two runs another 100 ft to a slung block; pitch three arrives at a large terrace known as Lunch Ledge. If three pitches have gone by and you have not reached an obviously large ledge, you are not on the line.

The named traverse pitch is well above Lunch Ledge. Everything below it is poor, loose rock, so bad rock low down does not mean you are lost — it is the one pitch of good rock that is the exception here, not the rule.
hazards: no established approach to the talus - the historic approach crosses private roads residents forbid
loose mossy slab scrambled unroped above the talus
a snow cone at the base of the slabs in early season
climber-triggered rockfall on the talus cone
poor rock quality on all but the traverse pitch

approach_variants.name: Sahale ski track and the south-side talus fans
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct as rock; also done in winter
approach_variants.notes:
Park somewhere along Alpental Road. Parking on the road near the Sahale Ski Club is sometimes possible, but it often is not and you may have to leave the car further away and walk. Respect the posted no-parking on the private sections.

From there head up the Sahale ski track toward Guye for roughly three quarters of a mile to a mile. Where the track starts to peter out, climb through the boulder field and a short band of slide alder to reach the base of the cliff.

Then traverse EAST along the base of the wall. You will pass Blood Sport on the way. Keep going until you reach a taller talus fan, and go up that fan to the cliff.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The taller talus fan east of Blood Sport is the marker, and it is a comparative one rather than a described one: it reaches noticeably higher up the wall than any of the talus you passed getting there. When the ground under you starts climbing the face rather than just banking against it, that is the fan you want.

Blood Sport itself is the negative marker. It is a bolted line at the base of the south wall — arriving at it tells you that you are on the right side of the mountain but have not traversed far enough east. Do not start up there.

If you are still on the ski track with the wall above and to your left, you have not yet reached the point where the track fades and you are below the traverse entirely.
hazards: rockfall on the talus and in the gullies
slide alder between the boulder field and the base of the cliff
limited and partly private parking on Alpental Road
the ski track fades rather than ending at a definite point, so the turn-off uphill is judged not signed

approach_variants.name: Cave Ridge saddle from Alpental
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct; also done as a winter scramble with axe and traction
approach_variants.notes:
From the Alpental / Snow Lake trailhead area (about 3,080-3,120 ft), take the unmarked climbers' boot path that leaves the pavement close to the Snow Lake trail sign — the one that serves Snoqualmie Mountain and Cave Ridge, not the west-face talus approach. Follow it up to the saddle between Cave Ridge and Guye Peak, roughly a mile and a half in and reported around 4,500-4,600 ft.

From the saddle, turn right (north) and work toward Guye's north summit. Helmets are worth wearing from the point you leave the trail; climber-triggered rockfall is common on the talus and in the gully.

This peak is also reached from the northbound PCT trailhead through Commonwealth Basin, which is the east side of the mountain — a different approach to a different aspect.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Cave Ridge / Guye saddle is your fix. From it, Guye's north summit is directly to your right and north, and a scramble gully runs from the saddle area up to a point just north of the north peak. It is very steep but reported as class 3 in summer. If you are at a col and the ground to the north is walkable ridge rather than a steep gully, you are looking at the wrong side of the saddle.

The decision point is around 4,840 ft, where the gully runs into a large rock face. Going RIGHT there leads into a moat, and parties have found it very awkward and had to reverse. Going LEFT — a steep snow traverse in season — is the better option. If you are fighting a moat against rock, you took the right-hand option: back off and cross left.

Higher, near the north summit, the Hidden Ridge variation traverses right to an outcrop where a horn can be slung for a single rappel of about 30 ft into the notch between the north and middle summits. That rappel into a notch is the confirmation you found the variation; without it you are on the ordinary scramble.
hazards: moat against a large rock face around 4,840 ft if you take the right-hand line
steep snow traverse on the left-hand bypass
climber-triggered rockfall on the talus and in the gully
very steep gully - class 3 in summer, considerably more serious under snow

approach_variants.name: Commonwealth Basin and Lundin Basin
approach_variants.season: Jun-Jul on snow is the good window; brushy and slow once melted out
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT-North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead off the Alpental road (about 3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; within roughly half a mile bear left onto the Commonwealth Basin use trail, which climbs gently along Commonwealth Creek through old-growth for about 1.7 miles as the valley opens out.

Near 4,200 ft leave the main Red Pass tread and cut west, contouring into Lundin Basin below Red Mountain's south face. From there climb a broad couloir — snow in early season, scree and talus by late summer — up the steep south side of Lundin to gain the West Ridge at its notch.

This is much the better line while snow still covers the basin: it buries the brush and the boulders, and parties report a long glissade on the way out. Once melted out the lower basin is brushy with steep scree and talus, and that is the reason many parties switch to the Cave Ridge approach late in the season.

Commonwealth Creek is reliable water low down; nothing above is dependable, so fill up in the basin.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Both approaches converge at the low notch on the West Ridge, near 5,800 ft, and that notch is where the technical climbing starts — nothing below it needs a rope.

Coming up from the basin, aim for a depression in the face beneath the notch. Climb easy class 3 ground up to that depression, then the slabby depression itself is the crux of the entry, class 4 to low fifth, and you bear RIGHT at the top of it to arrive in the notch. If you are climbing slab and it does not lead to a col within a rope length or two, you picked the wrong depression.

Negative markers. If you gained the crest somewhere that walks easily on both sides, you are on the ridge but past the notch and the climbing above will not match any description. And if you find yourself scrambling straight at the summit block instead of setting out along a ridge, you came up the south face rather than to the west ridge notch.

The ridge involves class 4 to mid fifth moves and wants rock gear. Do not attempt it wet.
hazards: wet-slide and sluffing in the south-face couloir under afternoon sun - axe, crampons if firm, early season
heavy brush and steep loose scree in the basin once the snow is gone
no reliable water above Commonwealth Creek
the ridge is unsafe wet and unsafe without rock gear

approach_variants.name: Cave Ridge traverse from Alpental
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Alpental day-use lot and find the unmarked, unmaintained Snoqualmie Mountain climbers' trail that starts about 50 ft south of the signed Snow Lake trailhead. It crosses below a small waterfall and climbs steeply through forest and slide alder.

At an unsigned split around 4,600 ft, paths fork toward Snoqualmie Mountain, Cave Ridge and Lundin. Take the Cave Ridge / Lundin fork, cross over Cave Ridge near its low notch, then follow an ascending climbers'-trail traverse below the ridge crest — staying on the Commonwealth Basin, north, side — to the West Ridge notch.

This skirts the brushy lower basin entirely, which is why parties prefer it once the snow has gone. There is no reliable water past the trailhead.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You arrive directly at the low notch on the West Ridge, around 5,800 ft, which is where the technical climbing begins. Arriving by this line you should be traversing beneath the crest on the north (Commonwealth) side and then step up into a col with the ridge rising to your right toward the summit.

If the traverse has you on the south side looking down into Lundin Basin, you have crossed the crest too early. If you top out on a walkable ridge with no notch, you have gone past.

As with the basin approach, the entry from below the notch goes class 3 to a slabby depression, then class 4 to low fifth up the depression, bearing right into the notch.
hazards: exposed and sometimes loose climbers'-trail traverse beneath Cave Ridge
early-season snow traverse on the crossing that can warrant an axe
unsigned trail split around 4,600 ft with three destinations
slide alder low down
no reliable water past the trailhead

approach_variants.name: PCT to Commonwealth Creek, then cross-country into the cirque
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; early season on snow is preferred
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snoqualmie Pass PCT-North trailhead off I-90 exit 52, about 3,000-3,040 ft. Follow the PCT northbound roughly 2.5 miles through second-growth, climbing gently, to the signed junction with the Commonwealth Creek Trail (#1033).

Follow #1033 into Commonwealth Basin. Not far past the junction it crosses Commonwealth Creek — the last reliable water on the approach, and a tricky ford in early season at high snowmelt.

Immediately beyond the crossing, leave the maintained tread. There is no trail from here. Climb cross-country to the northwest, first through open timber and then boulder and talus, into the open cirque at the headwaters of Commonwealth Creek beneath Lundin's south face.

An equivalent description used by many parties: stay on the Commonwealth Creek trail until soon after the stream crossing, where it starts moving up onto the flank of Red Mountain, then leave it and head northwest into the basin. Many climbers deliberately come early in the season, when snow covers the brush and boulders and the cross-country leg is quick.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The south face rises straight out of the head of the basin, and the route begins at the LOW POINT of the face, directly beneath the summit.

The way to get this right is to line yourself up by eye before you walk in: pick out the summit from the basin floor, drop that line to where it meets the bottom of the face, and walk to that point. Parties who instead head for the first inviting rock they reach end up starting left or right of the low point, and the climbing above does not match — the route runs several low-fifth pitches to a slab, with the final pitch steeper.

If the ground at the foot of your line rises noticeably before it meets rock, you are off to one side; the true start is where the face is lowest.

In poor visibility this is a hard place to be sure of yourself, because the basin is featureless talus and the face is continuous. The summit-to-toe line is the only test that works, so take the bearing while you can still see the top.
hazards: Commonwealth Creek ford in early season high flow
no trail from the creek crossing onward - open timber then boulder and talus
lingering snow patches in the upper basin into early summer
route-finding across talus to locate the true toe of the face

approach_variants.name: PCT to Commonwealth Creek, then cross-country into the cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the standard South Face approach. Snoqualmie Pass PCT-North trailhead (about 3,000 ft), PCT northbound roughly 2.5 miles to the Commonwealth Creek Trail (#1033) junction, then #1033 into Commonwealth Basin.

Shortly after the trail crosses Commonwealth Creek — the last water — leave the tread, either right there or after the path has begun to swing up onto Red Mountain's flank, and climb cross-country northwest into the upper basin beneath Lundin's south face.

Expect the same talus and boulder travel, and the same lingering early-season snow in the basin, as the standard route.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variation starts near the CENTRE and lowest point of the face, at an obvious layback hand-sized crack. The crack is the identifier, not the position — look for the feature itself.

This matters more here than on most routes: the variation does not start where Beckey's guidebook places the original South Face line, so a party trying to match an old topo photo will be put in the wrong place by the book. Find the layback crack near the low centre of the face and start there.

If you are on rock with no single obvious crack line, or the crack you have found is off toward one edge of the face rather than near its centre, keep looking along the base rather than committing.
hazards: Commonwealth Creek ford in early season high flow
no trail beyond the creek crossing
lingering early-season snow in the upper basin
published route topos disagree on where the line starts

approach_variants.name: Denny Creek to Melakwa Lake and the south ridge
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; the northwest-facing finish holds snow into June or July
approach_variants.notes:
Denny Creek trailhead (about 2,280 ft) via Forest Road 58 off I-90 exit 47. Take Denny Creek Trail #1014 up the valley. At roughly 1.2-1.3 miles it crosses Denny Creek at the Slippery Slab — smooth cascading bedrock and pools, and the last easy reliable water before the climb steepens.

Beyond the slab the trail climbs through forest, crosses talus, and switchbacks to Hemlock Pass around 3.8 miles and 4,600 ft, where it meets the Melakwa Lake Trail #1011 junction. Bear toward Melakwa Lake and descend gently about half a mile to the lake at roughly 4,550 ft — good campsites, and the last dependable water before the summit push.

From the lake, cross the outlet stream and pick up the well-defined but unmaintained climbers' bootpack on the ridge to the west (your left as you look up the lake). It climbs steeply through subalpine trees, heather and talus onto Kaleetan Knoll, Point 5,700.

The path then goes OVER that first prominence and drops several hundred feet down its west side into a rocky, west-facing talus bowl below the saddle separating Point 5,700 from Kaleetan's south ridge. Cairns mark that crossing. There is no continuous tread here, and the cairns are the first thing to disappear in cloud or early-season snow.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
After the talus crossing you regain the ridge at the saddle and follow the boot path north, just below or along the crest, for a few hundred yards. The start of the actual scrambling is an obvious gully and ledge system splitting Kaleetan's south face — roughly 400-600 vertical feet of class 2-3 on loose, exfoliating rock, exiting onto a short summit ridge with one more brief scramble to the true summit at 6,259 ft.

The test at the foot of it: you should be able to look up the whole length of the gully and see it exit onto ridge crest, not run out into more face. A gully that closes down against the wall above is not the one.

Two negative markers. If you are still descending, or still crossing talus with the ridge above and to your right, you have not yet regained the saddle and are too early — the boot path drops before it climbs. And if you began scrambling before you dropped off the west side of Point 5,700, you are on the wrong prominence; the knoll is a bump to be crossed, not the peak.

In cloud, the sequence to hold onto is: lake outlet, up to the knoll, OVER it and DOWN its west side, across the talus on cairns, regain the ridge at the saddle, then north a few hundred yards to the gully.
hazards: loose, exfoliating rock throughout the summit gully and upper ridge
snow lingering on the northwest-facing finish into June or July - trip reports carry axe and light traction
no continuous trail on the talus traverse below the saddle - cairn-following only, and useless in cloud
increasing exposure near the top
no dependable water above Melakwa Lake

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail to Glacier Meadows
approach_variants.notes:
Hoh Rain Forest trailhead (about 578 ft) inside Olympic National Park. The Hoh River Trail runs east; the first ten and a half miles to Lewis Meadows are gentle old-growth walking beside the braided river, with water the whole way. Past the Olympus Guard Station the High Hoh Bridge crosses the gorge and the ground steepens. Elk Lake sits around mile 15 at 2,500 ft, and the trail then climbs in earnest to Glacier Meadows at 4,200-4,300 ft, about mile 17.2-17.5, which is the standard base camp.

About a quarter mile below Glacier Meadows the trail crosses a washout on a ladder of roughly 100 ft with a fixed rope beside it. For many parties that is the hardest part of the walk in.

In early season there are several steep, consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows that want an axe and crampons.

A wilderness permit is required year-round for every overnight stay in Olympic National Park, obtained in advance through Recreation.gov or a Wilderness Information Center, and the Hoh is one of the areas that runs on a daily quota. Camping is not permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variant ends at camp, not at climbing. The confirmation you are at Glacier Meadows rather than somewhere short of it is the washout ladder and fixed rope just below it — if you have not climbed a ladder, you are still below.

From the meadows a way trail runs about 0.8 mile up onto the crest of the lateral moraine, a narrow exposed catwalk with loose rock underfoot, then follows the crest roughly another 0.2 mile before dropping onto the toe of the Blue Glacier. The drop onto the ice is where you rope up; nothing before it is glacier travel.
hazards: roughly 100 ft ladder plus fixed rope at the washout below Glacier Meadows
steep consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows in early season
narrow, loose lateral moraine crest with rockfall on the descent to the glacier toe
no camping permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier

approach_variants.name: Glacier Meadows to the summit block via Snow Dome and Crystal Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Rope up at the toe of the Blue Glacier and travel up to Snow Dome around 6,600-6,800 ft. This is roped crevasse travel throughout. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is often passable only on a snow bridge, and that bridge has to be scouted afresh each season.

Olympic National Park points climbers at the Crystal Pass line as the standard: from Snow Dome over Crystal Pass, then traversing immediately south of and below Five Fingers Ridge, over the false summit, and finally onto the true summit block of the West Peak. It is longer than the alternatives and generally regarded as the safer option through most of the season.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The only technical climbing on this route is the summit block of the West Peak, and finding it is the crux of the day, because THE TRUE SUMMIT IS NOT VISIBLE from the north side. A party that keeps navigating toward the highest thing it can see from Snow Dome ends up at the five-fingered false summit, which is EAST of where it wants to be.

The rule that works: go south-southeast through one of the two gaps to the LEFT, or far left, of the five fingers, and come at the summit from the east or southeast — approaching an objective you cannot yet see.

Once through, a rising traverse leads to a loose rocky gully; you go up that, over, and down into a second rocky gully, then up a final steep snow slope that delivers you to the foot of the block.

You are there when you are standing under a discrete rock tower roughly 80 ft high. The standard finish is class 4 on loose rocky ramps; there is also a line of about 80 ft straight up the north face on mostly solid rock, around 5.4. If you are under a snow slope with no rock tower above it, you have not arrived — keep going.

Expect a bergschrund or moat immediately below the block. Its state changes through the season and it can force a short detour or a stretch of short-roping; on the pinnacle just east of the West Peak parties have found a schrund below it and deteriorating scree above, and have grouped tightly or moved one at a time because of the rockfall.
hazards: crevasses throughout - a large crevasse near Crystal Pass often crossable only on a snow bridge that must be scouted each season
bergschrund or moat immediately below the summit block, variable through the season
loose deteriorating scree on the block and on the pinnacle east of it - rockfall onto your own party
the true summit is hidden from the north, so navigation is to a point you cannot see
the false summit is east of the true summit and catches parties out

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail and Blue Glacier to the West Ridge toe
approach_variants.notes:
The walk in is identical to the standard route: Hoh River Trail from the rain forest trailhead to Glacier Meadows at 4,200-4,300 ft, about 17.4-17.5 miles, including the ladder and fixed rope at the washout below the meadows. Then the way trail onto the lateral moraine crest and down onto the toe of the Blue Glacier, where you rope up.

Snow Dome at roughly 6,700-6,800 ft, about two miles of glacier travel above Glacier Meadows, is the recommended high camp for this route.

From Snow Dome, cross the Blue Glacier to the southwest WITHOUT gaining or losing much height, keeping Crystal Pass, Five Fingers Ridge and the West Peak in view as your three reference points.

A wilderness permit is required year-round for overnight stays in Olympic National Park and must be arranged in advance; the Hoh is a quota area.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The ridge is gained at a MOAT at its lowest point, close to 7,260 ft. That moat is the confirmation — it is a specific place, not a stretch of ridge, and whether it can be crossed changes through the season, so plan to inspect rather than assume.

Above the moat there is roughly 600 ft of ridge and then about 100 ft of summit block.

The negative marker is easy to spot and easy to ignore: if you are GAINING height toward Crystal Pass, you have drifted onto the standard route and are heading for the summit block from the east instead of for the toe of the ridge. The crossing to the West Ridge is essentially level.

The ridge itself is never harder than 5.4 and never easier than class 3. It can be protected the whole way but is run out in places.
hazards: moat at the ridge toe near 7,260 ft, condition varies through the season
crevasses on the southwest crossing of the Blue Glacier
runout protection on the ridge despite the moderate grade
snow bridges over the bergschrund below the direct summit line have collapsed as early as mid-July in some years

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips roadbed, Lake Constance trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; June snow makes the South Chute far pleasanter than late-summer scree
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-3.5 for the Lake Constance trail alone
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Dosewallips road washout around 600 ft, reached from US 101 at Brinnon on FR 2610. The road has been closed to vehicles since a washout in 2002, so the first 5-6 miles up the Dosewallips valley are on the old roadbed.

The Lake Constance climbers' path is signed but unmaintained and carries no Forest Service trail number — it is a boot path. It launches straight into root-and-branch pulling through old burn debris for the first 0.4 mile before the old growth closes in. At about 0.8 mile, Half Acre Rock is a large monolith with campsites beside Constance Creek and is the obvious rest and water stop; by late summer the creek and the canyon above it run dry, so treat it as the last reliable water below the lake.

Past 1.1 miles the brush opens onto steep exposed slopes, and by 1.3 miles the creek is forced through a defile and the path is pushed up and over a series of rock ledges and short cliff bands, using roots and a landmark Alaska cedar to gain the next ledge. Exposure increases with each one and a slip is serious.

All told it gains roughly 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles to Lake Constance at 4,680-4,800 ft, one of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics. Lake Constance is a reservable Olympic National Park backcountry site with reservations available roughly mid-June to mid-October; a wilderness permit is required for the overnight, and parties of seven or more must use the designated group sites.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the lake, follow the boot path around the shore, out onto a large scree cone, and north into Avalanche Canyon between Inner Constance and Mount Constance. A large rock called the Thumb sits on the canyon's left side; the South Chute lies on the south side of the Thumb, and due south of the Cat Ears.

The most useful rule on this mountain: START UP THE SOUTH CHUTE AS SOON AS THE CAT EARS COME INTO VIEW, not when the chute starts to look obvious. Entering low keeps you on firmer ground, where there is a path in places; parties who keep walking up the canyon and attack the chute higher get the worst of the loose scree. If the Cat Ears have been visible for a while and you are still walking north, you have overshot the entrance.

The chute climbs roughly 1,900 ft of scree to a saddle near 6,560-6,600 ft below the Cat Ears. Descend about 150 ft, then a second gully leads to a notch near 7,300 ft.

Above that is the exposed upper maze, and identifying which traverse you are on is the thing to get right. The Finger Traverse is a downsloping ledge above a cliff with old rusted pitons on it — the pitons are the identifier, and some parties clip them as a solo-belay anchor. The Terrible Traverse is a hard-snow traverse of roughly 45 degrees above a big cliff and a nasty drainage. Both feed into class 3, occasionally class 4, ground leading to the base of the summit block. If you are on a traverse and the summit block is not visible above and ahead of you, you are on the wrong ledge.

The actual climbing is only the summit block, about 60 ft, with the North Chimney taking its north side at 3rd class — reported by plenty of people as feeling like easy 4th.
hazards: fatal-fall exposure on both the Terrible and Finger Traverses
steep firm snow on the Terrible Traverse - several pickets advised in early season
exposed rock ledges and short cliff bands on the Lake Constance trail above 1.3 miles
loose talus and scree the length of Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
no water above the lake in late summer, and Constance Creek itself runs dry

approach_variants.name: Bike the closed Dosewallips roadbed
approach_variants.notes:
The 5-6 miles of closed roadbed between the washout and the Lake Constance path is old road surface rather than trail, and mountain-biking it is a common way to cut the walk at both ends of the trip. The bike is left at the unsigned start of the climbers' path.

Everything above that point is identical to the walk-in variant: the same unmaintained boot path, the same 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles, the same rock ledges and the same lake.

The same permit rules apply — a wilderness permit for the overnight at Lake Constance, reservable roughly mid-June to mid-October, with group sites required for parties of seven or more.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Unchanged from the walk-in: around the lake, north into Avalanche Canyon, and up the South Chute as soon as the Cat Ears appear above you, with the Thumb on the canyon's left marking the chute's south side. The Cat Ears becoming visible is the trigger to start climbing, not a landmark to walk toward.
hazards: old roadbed surface with washouts
everything above the bike drop is unchanged, including the exposed ledges on the Lake Constance path

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance and Avalanche Canyon to Crystal Pass
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once Crystal Pass and the lower arete have shed snow; firm early-season snow in the canyon is faster and safer than bare talus
approach_variants.hours: 3-4 from the lake to the pass
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as the standard route: the closed Dosewallips roadbed for roughly 5 miles, then the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail, which gains about 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles with no switchbacks and hand-over-hand pulling in places. Figure 2.5-3.5 hours on that section. Camp at the established sites at the north end of the lake; a wilderness permit is required and the site is reservable roughly mid-June to mid-October.

From the lake, take the boot path around its eastern shore, come out onto a large scree cone, traverse north across the cone and into Avalanche Canyon. Do NOT turn off into the South Chute — that is the standard route. Instead keep going north up the canyon, past the Thumb, roughly 1.5 miles of steady uphill to Crystal Pass at the canyon's head.

The canyon is loose, poorly consolidated talus and scree when snow-free and much faster on firm early-season snow; carry an axe June into July. The final few hundred feet to the pass steepen, there is often a remnant of ice below the scree fan leading up to it, and softening snow by mid-morning is a good argument for an early start.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no ambiguity at the top: the West Arete is the prominent ridge rising DIRECTLY out of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon, and it runs straight up to Constance's summit ridge crest. If you are standing in a windy col with the canyon behind you and a ridge going up on your right toward the summit, you are at the start.

The negative marker is a turn made much lower down. If you found yourself climbing a scree chute out of the west side of the canyon with the Cat Ears above you, you are on the standard South Chute route and will end up in the upper maze and the traverses, not on the arete. The arete approach never leaves the canyon floor until the canyon itself ends.

On the arete, the climbing stays close to the crest on broken class 2 and 3 with the odd class 4 or low fifth step, so easy ground at the start is correct here and is not a sign you are off route.
hazards: loose, poorly consolidated talus and scree the length of Avalanche Canyon when snow-free
steepening snow and an ice remnant below the scree fan at Crystal Pass
softening snow by mid-morning on the final slope to the pass
exposed rock ledges on the Lake Constance approach trail
cold wind at Crystal Pass
long committing approach with no water above the lake late season

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and the Brothers climbers' path (summer)
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; by late August the couloir is often scrambling rather than snow
approach_variants.notes:
Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25, around 700 ft. About 3 miles and 1,100 ft of gain on maintained trail through second- and old-growth, crossing several creek drainages, to Lena Lake at roughly 1,800 ft — a busy backpacking destination with a ranger station, and the last easy reliable water and camping before the climbers' route.

Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden Brothers boot path, which follows the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth known as the Valley of the Silent Men for roughly 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp around 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring. Most parties use this as high camp for a two-day ascent.

Route-finding gets hardest immediately after leaving camp for the summit push, where the boot path repeatedly appears to vanish. Follow a climbers' path upstream and west along the west fork for about a mile. It crosses an avalanche debris field where slide alder and downed logs — some with hand-lines or steps cut into them — hide the line, and creek fords may be needed. Beyond the debris field the path re-enters forest and climbs toward the couloir.

Water is reliable at the lake and up Lena Creek to high camp. Above camp there is nothing dependable once you are on scree and snow.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are at the base of the actual climb when the climbers' path fades out in a large meandering gully at the bottom of a broad debris and deposition fan, with the couloir narrowing above it — roughly 4,000-4,300 ft. The path ending is the marker; there is no cairn or sign.

Above that, two features tell you the route is going right.

The Hourglass, near 5,800 ft, is a narrow rock and snow constriction and the crux of getting to the summit block: a couple of exposed 3rd-to-4th class moves in summer, or a steep 35-45 degree snow neck in spring which can be a thin snow bridge and which opens a moat at its base as it melts.

Higher, at the top of the snow, there is a notch with a large rock in it. Climb AROUND that rock to the RIGHT to reach the scree gully beyond. The general rule reported by parties who lose the thread here is: when in doubt, go right.

Cairns exist most of the way, but several of them are misleading. Treat a cairn as a hint and the terrain as the authority. The final roughly 200 vertical feet to the true south summit is class 4 with real exposure.
hazards: avalanche debris field of slide alder and downed logs between high camp and the couloir, with possible creek fords
moat opening at the base of the Hourglass as the snow recedes
thin snow bridge through the Hourglass constriction in spring
misleading cairns on the upper route
class 4 with real exposure on the last 200 ft
no reliable water above high camp

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow ascent
approach_variants.notes:
The classic time for this route is early season, roughly April into May, because the gullies fill in with dense brush later and the snow-covered version is much faster.

The approach is the same — Lena Lake, the Brothers boot path up the East Fork, the climbers' camp near 2,900 ft — but the avalanche debris field between camp and the couloir is easier under snow, and the couloir itself becomes a snow climb requiring an axe and reliable self-arrest rather than a scree slog.

Snow also buries the boot path, so the route-finding difficulty immediately above camp is worse, not better: there is no tread to find at all.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The deposition fan at the foot of the couloir is still the mark, but under snow the fan and the couloir merge visually. Read it by width: the base is where the open fan narrows into a defined couloir line, several hundred feet of which you then climb before exiting onto its west side and continuing up toward the spur.

The Hourglass around 5,800 ft is the feature to inspect from below. In spring it is a steep snow neck at 35-45 degrees and is sometimes a thin snow bridge — a moat at its base is the sign it is going.

The notch with the large rock at the top of the snow is still passed on the RIGHT.
hazards: avalanche hazard in the couloir and on the approach slopes
thin or collapsing snow bridge at the Hourglass
steep 35-45 degree snow requiring axe and solid self-arrest
no boot path visible under snow above high camp

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness and Royal Basin to Gilhooley Saddle
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; before July is preferred while snow still covers the loosest ground
approach_variants.notes:
Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,500 ft, at the end of FR 2870; a Forest Service day-use pass is needed at the trailhead. Start on the Upper Dungeness Trail (FST 833), which climbs gently through old growth along the river. At around a mile it reaches Royal Creek and the junction with the Royal Basin Trail (FST 832) — bear right and south onto 832 and follow Royal Creek upstream.

The trail climbs gradually through forest, opens into rocky brushy ground above about 4,000 ft, and reaches Royal Lake at 5,100 ft roughly 6-7 miles in. That is the last easy reliable water and the usual overnight on a two- or three-day trip. Royal Lake runs on an Olympic National Park quota, so an overnight needs a wilderness permit arranged in advance.

From the lake, go around to its far end past Shelter Rock — a large pillow-lava overhang used as a rough bivy shelter — then through a meadow with a waterfall and along the outlet into Upper Royal Basin at 5,600-5,700 ft, about another mile and 500 ft. Good camping and snowmelt water there.

From the upper basin tarn, leave the trail and climb southwest across a glacial moraine, roughly a mile, then up a large snow slope — mud and scree once it melts out — on the west edge of Deception's northeast face, toward the Deception-Martin (Gilhooley) saddle and the remnant Deception Glacier. Helmets from the moraine up: the rock on the whole upper mountain is loose rotten pillow basalt, and parties above you will move it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The saddle is your fix, and it is a place to move through rather than rest — rockfall there is close to constant, and worst at its west end. Do not stop and rack up in it.

From the saddle, descend about 100 ft onto the glacier remnant and traverse WEST, around Gilhooley Tower and the crags beside it. Do not try to climb over the tower; go around it.

The confirmation you got around correctly is the ground itself: once you are on the slopes SOUTH of Gilhooley Tower, everything remaining to the summit is a walk on class 2 slopes. Easy ground means you are right. If instead you are on steepening rotten rock, you did not go far enough west — reverse and continue around.

From Deception Basin the scramble takes roughly three hours.

One route-finding trap worth naming: the alternative line through Surprise Basin avoids the steepest ground and is described by multiple trip reports as long, arduous and not worth taking. If your line has stopped feeling steep and has started feeling endless, check which basin you are in.
hazards: near-constant rockfall at Gilhooley Saddle, worst at its west end - do not loiter
rotten pillow basalt throughout the upper mountain, helmets mandatory from the moraine up
steep loose scree on the west side of the upper basin
rockfall triggered by parties above
steep, exposed and serious ground - early season before July is preferred while snow covers the loosest rock

approach_variants.name: Royal Basin to Deception Basin
approach_variants.season: Apr-Jun, while the gully still holds snow
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness / Royal Basin Trailhead at about 2,500 ft, hike the Upper Dungeness River Trail and then the Royal Basin Trail roughly 7 miles with about 2,500 ft of gain to Royal Lake, then continue about another mile into Upper Royal Basin at roughly 5,600 ft — a meadow and tarn basin ringed by Deception, Mystery, Fricaba and Hal Foss.

A Northwest Forest Pass is needed at the trailhead, and Royal Lake is an Olympic National Park quota area, so an overnight needs a wilderness permit arranged in advance.

From the upper basin, leave the trail and ascend scree and talus northwest into Deception Basin. From the flat in Deception Basin the scramble to the summit takes about three hours.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the flat in Deception Basin, climb scree and talus to the northwest and look for a LARGE ROCK BUTTRESS. Immediately right of that buttress there are TWO gullies. Take the LEFT (west) one.

The buttress is what identifies the pair — do not try to identify the gully on its own, because there is more than one gully-shaped thing in the basin. Left of two, immediately right of a big buttress.

Follow that gully system up to Mount Deception's east ridge, arriving roughly 150 yards southeast of the summit, then follow the ridge to the top. Reaching the ridge that close to the summit is the confirmation you took the right gully; topping out much further along the ridge means you were in the wrong one.

The Honeymoon variation proper takes a left-branching snow gully off the main line — climb nearly to the low point and then branch left. By late season that branch is largely melted out and the feature disappears. It is graded class 3 but is reported to feel harder than that.
hazards: loose rotten rock throughout the upper mountain
snow in the gully in early season, and the left-branching variation melts out by late season
scree and talus in the basin
steep and exposed ground on a peak generally described as serious
